figures.title: One request seen by three instruments
figures.caption: The client wall clock starts before the request reaches the engine and ends after detokenization, so it includes tokenization, admission, queueing, prefill, decode and client overhead. The engine's counters split the same request into 8 s of prefill and 2 s of decode, and time to first token is 8.2 s, a fifth of a second above prefill. The counters sum to ten seconds while the wall clock says eleven, and the missing second is where queueing, tokenization, detokenization and client overhead live.
figures.alt: Five lanes across six steps: arrival, queue, prefill, first token, decode and last token. The wall clock lane runs from zero to eleven seconds. The counters lane carries prefill at 8 seconds, time to first token at 8.2 seconds and decode at 2 seconds. The logs lane marks the request start, first token and request end. The tokens lane carries the prompt tokens, one emitted token, then the generated tokens. The gap lane marks 0.2 seconds at the first-token step.

data.note: 8 + 2 + 0.2 s is ten seconds; the wall clock says eleven. The 0.2 s is the sum of queueing, cache lookup and the first decode step, which the counters do not break down further. The remaining second is tokenization, admission, detokenization and the client's own overhead, which no counter separates. The illustration is schematic: the counters report means over a window, not one trace.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to follow one request through all three instruments.

steps.label: A request arrives with its prompt tokens. The wall clock starts at zero and the log records a start timestamp.
The scheduler queues it for an admission slot. Counters are monotonic sums and see nothing here; the wait is invisible to them.
Prefill runs 8 s and emits no text. Counters report prefill 8 s, which is a mean over a window rather than one trace.
The first token appears. Counters report TTFT 8.2 s, so 8.2 − 8 = 0.2 s is queueing, cache lookup and the first decode step; the gap lane holds it and no counter breaks it down.
Decode emits the reply over 2 s, and the token lane counts what came out.
8 + 2 + 0.2 s comes to ten seconds, and the wall clock says eleven. The remaining second is tokenization, admission, detokenization and client overhead, which no counter separates.

figures.title: Three tokens-per-second numbers that are not the same quantity
figures.caption: All three bars carry the unit tokens/s and none of them measures the same thing. Counter-derived decode divides generated tokens by decode seconds and approaches the batch-one ceiling, 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7 for a 70B model at four bits on a 3,350 GB/s card. End-to-end throughput divides every token in the request, prompt included, by the total request seconds, so it averages prefill in and reports less: two thirds of the ceiling is 2/3 × 95.7 = 63.8. Aggregate throughput at concurrency four reads the weights once for four rows, so it is 4 × 3,350 ÷ 35 = 383, and each stream still sees a quarter of it. Quoting one without saying which is the error.
figures.alt: Three bars in tokens per second. Counter-derived decode at batch one is 95.7, the memory-bound ceiling for a 70B model at four bits on a 3,350 GB/s card. End-to-end throughput is 63.8, two thirds of the ceiling, because prompt tokens and queueing are inside its denominator. Aggregate throughput at concurrency four is 383, four times the ceiling, and each stream receives a quarter of that.

data.note: The same run reports three rates because the denominator changes. Decode-only counts generated tokens over decode seconds; end-to-end counts every token over wall clock; aggregate counts the sum of streams over the same wall clock. The third bar is the short-context case, where the cache term is small. Add the cache and it shrinks: at a 100,000-token context one stream holds 100,000 × 327,680 = 32,768,000,000 bytes, four streams hold 131.07 GB, and 4 × 3,350 ÷ (35 + 131.07) = 80.7, below the batch-one ceiling.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to see why one card reports three rates.

steps.label: Decode-only, batch one: a 70B model at four bits reads 35 GB per step, so 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7 tokens/s is the ceiling. Generated tokens over decode seconds approaches it.
End-to-end: every token in the request, prompt included, over the wall clock. Averaging prefill in gives 63.8 tokens/s, about two thirds of the decode-only rate.
Aggregate at concurrency 4 on a short context: 4 × 3,350 ÷ 35 = 383 tokens/s, because one weight read serves all four rows. Each stream still gets a quarter of it.

Add the cache and the third bar shrinks. One stream at 100,000 tokens reads 100,000 × 327,680 = 32,768,000,000 bytes; four streams read 4 × 32,768,000,000 = 131,072,000,000 bytes, 131.07 GB. Then 4 × 3,350 ÷ (35 + 131.07) = 80.7 tokens/s, below the batch-one ceiling.
